Hello, Stranger

A Every day we meet people we don't know: in a queue, at a wedding, on the bus to school. Many of us find small talk — short, friendly conversation about unimportant things — difficult or boring. But scientists and travellers say that it matters more than we think.

B In 1923 the anthropologist Bronisław Malinowski gave this kind of talk a name: “phatic communion”. When we say How are you? or Nice day, isn't it?, we don't really want information — nobody expects a report from the doctor! These words have a different job: they show that we are friendly and happy to talk.

C In her book Watching the English (2004), the anthropologist Kate Fox says that for many English people the weather is the safest topic of all. A comment like Cold, isn't it? is really a way of saying hello, and the polite answer is to agree — even when you think it's quite warm.

D Greetings are different all over the world. In Japan, people bow, and a deeper bow shows more respect. In Thailand, people press their hands together and bend their heads a little. In France, friends kiss on the cheeks — one, two, three or even four times, depending on the region. And in Uzbekistan, many people put their right hand on their heart, and a greeting often comes with a list of questions: How are you? How is your family? Are you tired?

E Is talking to strangers worth it? In 2014, two researchers at the University of Chicago, Nicholas Epley and Juliana Schroeder, asked some train passengers to start a conversation with a stranger and others to sit in silence. Most people expected the conversation to be awkward. In fact, the talkers had a more pleasant journey than the passengers who sat alone.

F There is more good news. A 2018 study found a “liking gap”: after a first conversation, people believe that the other person liked them less than he or she really did. So next time you are standing next to a stranger, ask a question. They will probably like you more than you think.

2

Grammar · question forms

TUSHUNTIRISH — SAVOL SHAKLLARI

A be bilan savollar: (soʻroq soʻzi) + be + ega. Are you a student? · Where is your sister? · Why were you late? do qoʻshilmaydi: Do you are …? emas.

B Boshqa feʼllar bilan: (soʻroq soʻzi) + do / does / did + ega + feʼlning oddiy shakli. Where do you live? · Does she know Ana? · What did you study? does va did dan keyin feʼlga -s ham, -ed ham qoʻshilmaydi: Does she work …? — Does she works? emas.

C Soʻroq soʻzlari: who · what · where · when · why · which · whose · how often · how much + sanalmaydigan ot (How much rent …?) · how many + koʻplik (How many languages …?) · what kind of … What … like? narsani tasvirlab berishni soʻraydi, yoqtirishni emas: What was the party like? — It was great!

D Istisnolar. Predlog oxirida qoladi: Where are you from? · Who do you live with? · What are you talking about? can, will, should bilan ham do ishlatilmaydi: Can you speak Russian?

DIQQAT — KOʻP UCHRAYDIGAN XATOLAR

1 ✗ Where you live? → ✓ Where do you live? — egadan oldin do / does / did.

2 ✗ Do you are married? → ✓ Are you married? — be bilan do ishlatilmaydi.

3 ✗ Does she works in a bank? → ✓ Does she work …? — does dan keyin -s yoʻq.

4 ✗ What means “rude”? → ✓ What does “rude” mean?

5 ✗ How many money do you earn? → ✓ How much money …? — money sanalmaydi.

MY COUSIN'S WEDDING

Last Saturday my cousin Aziza got married in Samarkand, and it was a wonderful day. The weather was perfect — sunny, but not too hot. The hall looked amazing, and Aziza's dress was gorgeous. The plov was delicious, of course, and the cake was all right — a bit too sweet for me. Aziza looked beautiful. Not everything was lovely, though. I talked about all four points. My questions had the right word order. I didn't read whole sentences.

MODEL — AN OPINION TEXT

Should people use their phones when they are with friends?

Have you ever talked to a friend who was looking at a phone the whole time? In my opinion, we shouldn't use our phones when we are with friends.

Firstly, it is rude. It shows the other person that the phone is more interesting than they are. Secondly, we miss a lot. Last month I had dinner with my cousins, and two of them were on their phones all evening — they didn't hear any of Grandma's wonderful stories.

Of course, sometimes a call is important, and then we have to answer it. But most of the time, the phone can wait. Our friends can't.
